articles.title: Who's talking, and what do they gain?

body.support:
The same thing can sound very different, depending on who's talking.

**Perspective.** Everyone sees things their own way. A skater and a café owner will see a new skate park differently. That's normal.

**Bias.** **Bias** is when someone only tells one side. They leave things out.

**Follow the money.** What does the person **gain** if you believe them?

- A **company** wants you to buy.
- A **paid creator** gets money or free stuff.
- A **mate** usually gains nothing.

**Influencers.** Lots of posts are paid ads. Creators should say so clearly: **Ad**, **Sponsored** or **Paid partnership**. Tiny tags like *#spon* at the end aren't clear.

**Discount codes** often pay the creator.

**Signs of bias**

- only good points
- no downsides or prices
- other views left out.

**We have bias too.** We believe people we like. That's why companies pay them.
body.core:
The same product, place or issue can sound completely different depending on who's talking.

**Perspective.** Everyone has a **perspective**: the way they see things, shaped by their age, job, background and experiences. A skater, a café owner and a parent will see a new skate park differently. That's normal.

**Bias.** **Bias** is when someone leans so far one way that they leave things out, twist the facts, or only tell you the good (or bad) side. A biased text isn't always lying. But it isn't giving you the full picture.

**Follow the money.** Ask: what does this person **gain** if I believe them?

- A **company** wants you to buy.
- A **paid creator** gets money, free products or a commission.
- A **political group** wants your vote or support.
- A **mate** usually gains nothing, but might just be excited.

People who gain have a **vested interest**. It doesn't mean they're wrong. It means you should check.

**Influencers and ads.** Lots of social media posts are paid ads that don't look like ads. In Australia, creators should make it **clear** when a post is an ad: words like **Ad**, **Advertisement**, **Sponsored**, **Paid partnership** or **Gifted**, up front, where you'll see them. Vague tags like *#sp* or *#spon* at the end of a long list of hashtags aren't clear.

Watch for **affiliate links** and **discount codes** too. If you use them, the creator usually gets paid.

**Signs of bias**

- only good points (or only bad points)
- no downsides, prices or problems mentioned
- strong emotive words, but few facts
- other views missing or made to look silly.

**Audiences have bias too.** We tend to believe people we like and follow. That's exactly why companies pay them.
body.extend:
The same product, place or issue can sound very different depending on who's talking.

**Perspective.** Every author and speaker has a **perspective**. It's shaped by their age, job, culture and experience. A skater, a nearby café owner and a parent will see a new skate park differently. You can't avoid having a perspective.

**Bias.** **Bias** is when a perspective bends the story. The author leaves out important facts, picks only the facts that help them, or makes other views look silly. A biased text can be true in parts and still mislead you overall.

**Vested interests.** Ask what the author gains if you believe them. Companies want sales. Paid creators get fees, free products or commission. Campaign groups want support. A **vested interest** doesn't make a claim false, but it means you should check it.

**Disclosure.** Lots of social media content is paid promotion made to look like a normal post. In Australia, creators are expected to **disclose** paid relationships clearly, using plain labels like *Ad*, *Sponsored*, *Paid partnership* or *Gifted*, where people will see them. Vague tags like *#sp* or *#spon*, buried in hashtags, aren't clear enough. **Affiliate links** and discount codes also show that money is involved.

**Signs of bias:** only one side, no downsides or costs, strong emotive words with little evidence, and other views missing or mocked.

**Audiences are biased too.** We tend to trust people we like and follow. That's exactly why brands pay influencers.

caseStudies.title: 81% of influencers checked

body.support:
The **ACCC** protects Australian shoppers. People complained about influencers who didn't say they were being paid.

In **2023**, the ACCC checked **118 influencers** on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and more.

- **81%** had posts that raised concerns.
- The biggest problem: not saying they were paid or got free stuff.
- Some used tiny tags like **“spon”** instead of saying **sponsored**.
- Fashion influencers were the worst: **96%**.

Why does it matter? We trust creators we like. That's why brands pay them. If you don't know it's an ad, you can't judge it.
body.core:
The **ACCC** is the government body that protects Australian consumers. People had complained to it about influencers who didn't say when they were being paid.

So in **early 2023**, the ACCC checked the posts of **118 influencers** across **Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook and Twitch**. It published what it found in **December 2023**.

- **81%** of the influencers had made posts that raised concerns about possibly misleading advertising.
- The most common problem was **not disclosing** a relationship with a brand: being paid, getting free products, or earning commission.
- Many used vague tags like **“sp”** or **“spon”** instead of clearly saying **sponsored**.
- Fashion influencers had the highest rate: **96%**. Gaming and tech was **73%**.

The ACCC said it would publish guidance for influencers and businesses, and warned it might take action where problems continued.

Why does it matter? When a creator you trust says they love something, you're more likely to buy it. That trust is exactly what brands are paying for. If you don't know a post is an ad, you can't judge it properly.
body.extend:
The **ACCC** (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) is Australia's consumer watchdog. It had received complaints about paid social media posts that weren't labelled as ads.

In **January and February 2023**, it checked posts by **118 influencers** on **Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook and Twitch**. It published what it found in **December 2023**.

- **81%** had made posts that raised concerns about possibly misleading advertising.
- The most common problem was **not disclosing** a link with a brand: being paid, getting free products, or earning commission.
- Many used vague labels like **“sp”** or **“spon”** instead of clearly saying **sponsored**.
- Concerns were highest for fashion influencers (**96%**). For gaming and tech, it was **73%**.

The ACCC said it would publish guidance for influencers and businesses, and warned it might take action.

This is really about perspective and position. Followers trust the creators they watch, and brands pay for that trust. Without clear labels, followers can't see the creator's commercial position, so they can't judge the post fairly.

model.text:
**Post 1:** A gamer shows off a new headset.
**Disclosure:** “#ad” at the very end of a long caption. It is hard to see.
**Whose side?** The brand's. She is paid to post.

**Post 2:** A mechanic reviews a cheap tool set.
**Disclosure:** He says, “I bought these myself.” There are no links.
**Whose side?** The viewer's. He also shows what broke.

**Post 3:** A food creator at a new café.
**Disclosure:** “Invited”. The meal was free.
**Whose side?** Partly the café's. A free meal can make a review kinder.

**Pattern:** The clearer the label, the more I trust the post.

teacher.overview: Students learn the difference between perspective (unavoidable) and bias (one-sided, omitting or distorting), how vested interests shape what speakers and authors say, how to spot sponsored content and judge whether it's clearly disclosed, and that audiences have biases too. They annotate a made-up influencer post, sort speakers, map perspectives on an e-scooter issue, and audit five real posts in their own feed. The case study is the ACCC's 2023 influencer sweep: of 118 influencers checked across six platforms, 81% had posts raising concerns, most often for not clearly disclosing brand relationships.
prep: Collect a few screenshots of sponsored posts (clearly and unclearly labelled) for students without access to social media.
Remind students to keep their feeds private when sharing; screenshots only.
Optional: the ACCC's guidance for influencers.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** everyone has a perspective; bias leaves things out or twists them. Company: sales; paid creator: money, free products, commission; mate: usually nothing. Ad, Advertisement, Sponsored, Paid partnership, Gifted.

**Post:** 1 who's talking (big audience); 2 emotive caption; 3 one-sided claim; 4 discount code and link (commission); 5 hidden label (#spon); 6 mixed message (says not an ad).

**Sort:** government site — fair; energy drink company — biased; mate — fair; streamer partnership — biased; car ad — biased; crash testers — fair.

**Perspectives (examples):** hire company — e-scooters are green and popular; gains customers, loses if banned. Older pedestrian — footpaths feel unsafe; gains safety from a ban. Doctor — sees injuries; gains fewer emergency cases.

**Case study:** to keep posts feeling authentic and keep sponsors; it shows the creator's commercial position, so you weigh it differently; answers will vary.
